newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: U.S., allies break ground for North Korea project.
newsitem.headline: U.S., allies break ground for North Korea project.

text.p: A consortium of capitalist nations broke ground on Tuesday for a landmark nuclear project in communist North Korea that Washington and Seoul have said is key to preserving peace on the peninsula.

Puffs of pink, green, orange and yellow smoke belched from a hillside in the northeastern town of Kumho as officials of the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) triggered a "symbolic blast".

KEDO is an international consortium, led by the United States, South Korea and Japan, responsible for financing the construction of two 1,000-megawatt light-water reactors in North Korea at an estimated cost of $4.5 billion to $5 billion.
The reactors are to be built over the next seven to 10 years in return for Pyongyang's 1994 promise to freeze and eventually dismantle its suspected atomic weapons programme.
Witnesses said diplomats from nine nations and the European Union put on white gloves and released a barrage of confetti and streamers as fireworks cascaded from the hillside.
They were among 200 people at the ground-breaking ceremony, which also included journalists and South Korean contractors.

"We have now reached a major new milestone: ground breaking for the light-water reactor project," U.S. President Bill Clinton said in a statement read by U.S. Ambassador Paul Cleveland shortly before the blast.
"Construction of the light-water reactors will contribute significantly to peace and stability of the Korean peninsula."
Stephen Bosworth, the U.S. executive director of KEDO, said Tuesday's ceremony established the credibility of the consortium and the nations leading it.
"This ground-breaking ceremony...marks the fulfilment of a promise -- a promise made over two years ago by the Republic of (South) Korea, Japan and the United States," he said.
Clearing of land at Kumho should have started more than a year ago but the signing of a KEDO-Pyongyang contract for the supply of the reactors was delayed for about eight months.
Heightened tensions on the peninsula after the grounding last September of a North Korean submarine on a southern beach also put KEDO's work on hold for several months.
Chang Sun-sup, chief South Korean representative for the project, said the ground-breaking served as "a catalyst for reconciliation and cooperation" with the reclusive North.
"It is the promising product of a concerted international effort," he said.

KEDO, formed in 1995 by Washington, Seoul and Tokyo under a U.S.-North Korean agreement in 1994, was later expanded to include Australia, Canada, Chile, Finland, Indonesia, New Zealand and the European Union.
South Korea, which is paying for most of the project, brought to Kumho 9,000 tonnes of earth-moving equipment which roared to life when the symbolic blast went off.
Bosworth told reporters that the project was "a bargain" considering what the international community would gain.

The West had suspected that Pyongyang had secured enough plutonium from its experimental graphite-moderated reactor to build nuclear bombs and feared the North could try to sell them to a terrorist group to earn the hard currency needed to rescue the impoverished state from an economic crisis.

North Korea has pledged to allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to conduct special inspections of all its nuclear facilities to determine it had not hidden any weapons-grade plutonium that could be used to make a bomb.
Joel Wit, deputy director of the U.S. State Department's Office of Korean Affairs, said this must take place before KEDO puts in the reactor cores at Kumho.
"If they don't come clean, they get a concrete building and that's it."
Lee Ki-won, vice president of the private Institute of North Korea Studies in Seoul, said the KEDO project could prompt Pyongyang to open up and seek cooperation with Seoul.
"This will be a pilot project for both sides and future cooperation will depend largely on its outcome," he said.
The two Koreas have been locked in a Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War.
